KEY MESSAGE 1...A coastal low will bring a period of moderate to heavy
rain and breezy to gusty winds this evening through early 
Monday morning. Potential for brief nuisance urban flooding. 

Current radar and analysis data show a developing/strengthening 
low pressure off the Mid-Atlantic coast accompanied by outer 
bands of rain. This low is expected to continue to track north 
into this evening, eventually passing near the Cape and Islands 
very early Monday morning. Within the southerly flow, a plume of
above normal moisture, 290-330 percent of normal, will surge 
northward ahead of the approaching coastal low by this evening. 
This will prime the environment for heavy rainfall once the 
better forcing/instability arrive with the low. As the plume of 
moisture arrives, showers will increase from south to to north 
late late this afternoon into the evening. Model guidance 
continues to highlight this system as fairly progressive with 
rain departing by mid-morning Monday. 

There has been a consistent east shift in the track in the coastal 
low across model guidance over the past 24 hours. This has 
shifted the greater risk for gusty winds east and the axis of 
higher rain totals(1-3") east as well. Deterministic and 
ensemble guidance show a general consensus with the swath of the
1-3" amounts oriented SW-NE across portions of RI into 
southeast MA. A subtle track shift may teeter this axis a little
east or west which has been reflected in across guidance even 
this close to the event. This shift has also decreased forecast
rain totals across west/central MA and CT with likely less than
0.50" in those areas. Given the progressive nature of this 
system, the risk for widespread flash flooding is low. However, 
the combo of very anomalous PWATs, frontogenetical 
forcing/convergence from offshore LLJ, and marginal instability 
should provide support localized heavier rain rates. Guidance 
highlights generally a 6-hr window late tonight into very early 
Monday morning for higher rain rates with potential for 1-2" in 
that timeframe. The REFS PMM QPF highlights potential for 
localized 3.0+ amounts across southeast MA. Given it's the only 
set of guidance hinting at this, it is more low prob or very 
localized. Additionally, based on 6 hr FFG, this doesn't appear 
to be a large threat. If the heavier rain positions closer to 
more flood prone areas such as New Bedford/Fall River this will 
require monitoring for minor flood impacts. For the most part, 
this will be mainly nuissance-type flooding/ponding in the poor 
drainage areas. 

Due to the eastward shift in storm track, the highest probabilities 
for stronger gusty winds will be confined to the coastal waters and 
at most the Cape and Islands. This will be supported by the strong 
pressure gradient with the low with a 45-60 kt southerly LLJ 
positioned across the coastal waters. There is still some degree of 
uncertainty in the expected magnitude of gusts with subtle 
differences in track across model guidance. In addition this is 
occurring overnight where there will be an inversion which will
limit full mixing. Ensemble probabilities show 40-60% 
probabilities for gusts 40 mph or greater across the outer 
coastal waters & Nantucket and 20-45% for Cape Cod. Gusts 20-40 
mph are most likely tonight with the highest for the Cape and 
Islands. CAA with an approaching cold front pushes into southern
New England over the course of Monday afternoon/evening. The 
steepened lapse rates will help bring another "push" of gusty 
winds out of the WNW with gusts 20-30 mph over the higher 
terrain.

Despite the higher astronomical tides, the progressive nature of 
this system will lower the risk for coastal flooding impacts for the 
Mon high tide. Coastal flood guidance shows surge around 1 ft, maybe 
a little above that during the Mon high tide window. By that point, 
winds will have decreased with direction shifted westerly with the 
lower pressure exited with the coastal low. This should mitigate 
coastal flood impacts. Splashover to very minor coastal flooding 
(reasonably worst case) possible for Nantucket, Cape, and east 
coast. 

KEY MESSAGE 2...Dry & colder weather follows Tue into Wed with 
highs mainly in the 40s. Lows Tue night mainly in the upper 
teens & 20s.

Monday's cold front ushers in a much colder and drier airmass for 
Tuesday and Wednesday as high pressure builds into the Great Lakes 
on Tuesday and New England on Wednesday. Cold advection drops 925mb 
temps from near ~11C on Monday to -3C Tue-Wed. Despite abundant 
sunshine this will limit high temps to the 40s while good 
radiational cooling gives us a very cold start to Wednesday...in the 
teens (high elevations) and 20s. 

KEY MESSAGE 3...Increasing confidence in an impactful storm around 
Thanksgiving. Heavy rain, strong winds, dangerous marine conditions, 
and coastal flooding are all potential hazards.  

Confidence is increasing that the northeast will be impacted by a 
strong storm
